toc.title: This moment may never happen again

blocks.p: My little family and I were in San Jose, California, for a huge family get-together, almost a reunion. My uncle turned 80, so my aunts, my uncles, my cousins all got together, people I hadn't seen in years. It's an Italian family, so things were very loud, and there were lots of hugs and smiles to go around. We met up at, of course, an Italian restaurant, Maggiano's in San Jose. So there was lots of food to go along with the smiles and the hugs and the loudness.

It's the next morning, and my little family and I slept in until 6:30 a.m. My wife woke me up by grabbing my foot and shaking it. My wife, my son, and I ate the continental breakfast at the hotel while my daughter slept in a little longer.

Then we went back up to the room. I was sitting on a bench, eating an apple, just processing. I was thinking about the night before, the conversations, and reflecting on my life, my upbringing, the conversations I had with my brothers, and how my wife and I are raising our own children.

So I was sitting quietly on the bench in the hotel room, processing, and then a balloon came out of the hotel sky, slowly lowering itself toward me, as a balloon would do. As it was lowering, my son said, "Hit it back."

And I felt a wave of irritation come over me. Why irritation? Honestly, I don't know, and it really doesn't matter. Maybe it was because my processing was interrupted while I sat on the bench quietly, in peace. Maybe I was irritated all along that morning and only realized it in that moment. Or perhaps my son's command, and the pressure of hitting the balloon before it touched the ground, brought me out of safety, through flight, and into fight in that split second.

I don't know. And again, it does not matter. What matters is that between the moment my son said "Hit it back" and the moment the balloon was about to bounce off my bald head, I did indeed hit it back. In that fraction of a second, a thought came to me, along with the irritation I was feeling.
The thought was: this moment may never happen again.

Did I think this thought and then shift my state out of irritation? Or did the sound of my son's voice trigger enough safety that my thought changed on its own? Interesting question, but again, it doesn't really matter. The thought came, and so did the playfulness to snap out of my processing and hit it back to him.

If you have not had the opportunity to hit a balloon back and forth with somebody recently, you are missing out. It's the most peaceful and playful thing you can do, I swear. But it could also be the most competitive and playful thing you can do, maybe especially with a kid. I've heard there's actually a professional sport of balloon hitting called keepie-uppie, something like that.
That moment will likely happen again. He's a 10-year-old boy, and I think I have a few more years of balloon hitting left. But maybe not. You never know.

My daughter and I hit balloons for quite a while. I think she's grown out of that by now. Although maybe if I just hit one to her and said, "Hey, hit it back," she'd snap out of it and hit it back, even though she's a very independent sixteen-and-a-half-year-old. I'll have to experiment with that. But it might not happen again. You never know.
The moment of my wife shaking my foot may never happen again either. I think it will. We tend to wake each other up with touch. But you never know, do you?

blocks.h: This moment may never happen again

blocks.p: I don't know how this relates to you and your life. But if you ever have the chance to hit a balloon back, make sure you do. Even if you'd rather sit and process while eating an apple, that moment may never happen again.

I don't mean this in a morbid way, although that is a reality as well. I mean it in a literal sense: that opportunity to connect in that way, that opportunity to be playful in that manner, may simply not come up again, and you'll miss out.
So consider this me hitting a balloon to you, with a smile on my face.
